title: Batching Defaults Workload Corpus v1 (Perf + Quality Gating)
author: Jonas Weber
body:
## Purpose
This page defines **Workload Corpus v1**, the representative set of request traces and synthetic workloads used to:
1) benchmark tiered batching defaults (fast / standard / cost-efficient) in the performance suite, and
2) gate changes to batching defaults through quality regression checks.

The intent is to make batching behavior **workload-aware** while keeping evaluation stable, repeatable, and meaningful across model families, GPU SKUs, and streaming vs non-streaming routes.

**Non-goals:**
- Building a fully per-customer custom corpus (beyond the beta cohort and internal service traces).
- Measuring business KPI outcomes directly (we measure latency, throughput, $/token proxies, and quality metrics).

---

## Corpus composition (overview)
Workload Corpus v1 is divided into **perf workloads** and **quality workloads**. Some artifacts are shared (e.g., prompt sets), but the execution configuration differs.

### Included route types
- Chat / text generation (streaming and non-streaming)
- Tool/function-calling style chat (structured output)
- Long-context chat and summarization
- Embeddings
- (Optional for perf only) rerank/classification-style short decode

### Why this mix
Batching defaults can change:
- **queueing behavior** (tail latency vs throughput)
- **token cadence** (streaming feel)
- **timing-dependent nondeterminism** (sampling variance and early-stop behavior)

We therefore need:
- realistic prompt-length and output-length distributions,
- concurrency sweeps and burst patterns,
- streaming cadence checks,
- long-context and memory-pressure stress,
- a minimal quality suite that is robust to minor timing differences.

---

## Data sources and privacy
### Sources
Workload Corpus v1 is built from:
- **Anonymized internal Redwood traffic** (hosted API + internal dogfood services) aggregated into length histograms and representative traces.
- **Synthetic prompts** authored internally for coverage of edge cases (tool calls, long-context, refusal/safety boundaries, JSON formatting).
- **Publicly available text** for long-context summarization and extraction tasks (licensed/permissible sources only), converted into prompt templates.

### Privacy constraints
- No raw customer content is stored in this corpus.
- Any internal traces are **content-stripped** and represented as:
  - token-length sequences,
  - structural markers (e.g., “system”, “user”, “assistant”, “tool”),
  - coarse categories (e.g., “customer_support”, “coding_assistant”),
  - timing metadata (arrival gaps) where needed.

### Storage and access
- Canonical corpus artifacts live under Applied ML & Evals and are used by perf-canary and the benchmark-lab runner.
- Access: internal only. If a future version includes customer-provided prompts under NDA, that subset will be marked **restricted** and separated.

---

## Canonical workload units
Each workload unit is described by:
- **Route type**: chat | completions | embeddings | rerank
- **Streaming**: true/false
- **Prompt shape**: prompt token length distribution + chat turns
- **Output shape**: expected generation token distribution and stop reasons
- **Concurrency model**: steady-state + burst parameters
- **Request mix weight**: % of total requests in a mixed run

We define two execution modes:
- **Perf mode:** measures latency/throughput/cost proxies under concurrency
- **Quality mode:** measures output stability and task metrics on fixed prompts

---

## Workload catalog (v1)
### W1 — Chat (short, streaming)
**Purpose:** token cadence sensitivity + low-latency tier validation.
- Route: chat
- Streaming: true
- Prompt tokens (p50/p90/p99): 220 / 520 / 900
- Turns: 3–8 (median 5)
- Output tokens (p50/p90/p99): 120 / 260 / 480
- Stop reasons: stop (90%+), length (rare)
- Mix weight: 20%

Representative categories:
- lightweight product Q&A
- "assistant drafting" short edits
- short coding questions

### W2 — Chat (medium, non-streaming)
**Purpose:** common API usage, stable overall throughput measurement.
- Route: chat
- Streaming: false
- Prompt tokens: 450 / 1,100 / 2,000
- Turns: 2–6
- Output tokens: 220 / 520 / 900
- Mix weight: 20%

### W3 — Tool-calling / structured output (streaming)
**Purpose:** validates batching does not break structured output cadence; catches timing-induced tool-call variability.
- Route: chat (tool calling enabled)
- Streaming: true
- Prompt tokens: 600 / 1,400 / 2,800
- Turns: 4–10
- Output tokens: 80 / 180 / 320 (assistant) + tool payload sizes in bytes (p50 0.8KB, p90 3KB)
- Mix weight: 10%

Notes:
- Includes JSON schema constrained outputs and function-call argument objects.
- Quality mode uses deterministic decoding (temperature=0) for most cases.

### W4 — Long-context summarization (non-streaming)
**Purpose:** prefill-heavy behavior; KV/cache and memory pressure interactions; queue delay guardrails.
- Route: completions or chat
- Streaming: false
- Prompt tokens: 4,000 / 12,000 / 28,000
- Output tokens: 300 / 900 / 1,600
- Mix weight: 10%

Task shapes:
- summarize meeting transcript / policy doc
- extract bullet points
- answer questions from long context

### W5 — Long-context chat (streaming)
**Purpose:** worst-case for perceived responsiveness; validates fast tier decode prioritization.
- Route: chat
- Streaming: true
- Prompt tokens: 8,000 / 18,000 / 30,000
- Turns: 6–14
- Output tokens: 120 / 300 / 700
- Mix weight: 5%

Cadence checks are emphasized here (see “Streaming cadence metrics”).

### W6 — Embeddings (short + medium)
**Purpose:** ensures tiered batching defaults don’t degrade embedding throughput/latency; checks batching across many small items.
- Route: embeddings
- Streaming: false
- Input tokens (single item): 40 / 180 / 650
- Batch cardinality (items/request): 1–64 (median 8)
- Mix weight: 25%

### W7 — Embeddings (large payload / document chunks)
**Purpose:** stress memory bandwidth and batch formation for bigger embedding items.
- Route: embeddings
- Input tokens: 250 / 900 / 1,800
- Items/request: 1–16 (median 4)
- Mix weight: 5%

### W8 — Rerank / short decode (perf-only)
**Purpose:** catches regressions in very short decode paths where queue delay dominates.
- Route: rerank (or short completion)
- Streaming: false
- Prompt tokens: 120 / 320 / 700
- Output tokens: 8 / 16 / 32
- Mix weight: 5%

---

## Prompt length histograms (aggregate)
The following histograms are used to validate that synthetic prompts reflect observed distribution (no raw text stored).

### Chat prompt length buckets (tokens)
- 0–256: 22%
- 257–512: 21%
- 513–1,024: 26%
- 1,025–2,048: 18%
- 2,049–4,096: 8%
- 4,097–8,192: 3%
- 8,193–16,384: 1.5%
- 16,385–32,768: 0.5%

### Embeddings input length buckets (tokens)
- 0–64: 35%
- 65–128: 22%
- 129–256: 20%
- 257–512: 14%
- 513–1,024: 7%
- 1,025–2,048: 2%

**Guardrail:** If a proposed corpus update changes any bucket by >5 percentage points, it requires Applied ML + SRE review (to avoid “moving the goalposts” in perf gating).

---

## Concurrency + arrival model
For perf runs, each workload is evaluated under three arrival patterns.

### A) Steady-state
- Constant request rate producing stable queueing
- Used to measure p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, GPU utilization

### B) Burst
- 30s burst at 3× steady-state, then 90s recovery
- Used to validate admission control + overload protection interactions with cost-efficient tier

### C) Diurnal jitter (synthetic)
- Inter-arrival times sampled from a log-normal distribution (CV tuned per workload)
- Used to avoid overfitting to perfectly periodic arrivals

Concurrency sweep points are selected per model size class (e.g., small/medium/large) and GPU SKU; the methodology page defines the exact sweep grid.

---

## Streaming cadence metrics (required for streaming workloads)
For streaming workloads (W1, W3, W5), we record:
- **TTFT (time to first token)**
- **Inter-token gap p50/p95** for tokens 1–32 and 33–128 (early vs steady decode)
- **Cadence stall rate**: % of responses with any gap >750ms (configurable by tier)
- **Client-visible jitter**: p95 of (max gap within first 30 tokens)

Cadence is assessed both at:
- server emission timestamps, and
- client receive timestamps in the harness (to capture buffering effects).

---

## Quality evaluation subset (v1)
Batching changes can cause slight differences even under the same sampling config due to timing and scheduling. The v1 quality suite is therefore designed to be:
- **mostly deterministic** (temperature=0 for many prompts),
- **metric-based** where possible (JSON validity, exact-match, constrained schema checks),
- **paired A/B** to catch drift.

### Q1 — Structured output validity (tool calling)
- 300 prompts
- Metrics:
  - JSON parse success rate
  - schema validation pass rate
  - tool-call selection stability (exact match under deterministic decode)

### Q2 — Long-context faithfulness checks
- 120 prompts (summarization + Q&A from long context)
- Metrics:
  - citation/quote presence rate (where applicable)
  - extractive answer overlap (token F1 vs reference spans)

### Q3 — General chat regression screen
- 400 prompts
- Metrics:
  - refusal policy markers (binary checks)
  - formatting checks (markdown tables, bullet list constraints)
  - lightweight LLM-as-judge (optional; not used as sole gate)

### Q4 — Embeddings invariance smoke test
- 1,000 inputs
- Metrics:
  - cosine similarity distribution between baseline and candidate (expect near-identity when embedding model unchanged)
  - outlier rate: % pairs with cos_sim < 0.999 (threshold configurable by model; track trend)

**Important:** Quality gates and thresholds are specified in the guardrails page; this page only defines the workload inputs.

---

## Execution matrix (what runs where)
### Perf canary (CI / nightly)
- Runs W1–W8 under fast/standard/cost-efficient tiers for a small set of model/SKU pairs.
- Must complete within CI time budget.
- Emits tier comparison tables and fails on defined regression thresholds.

### Benchmark-lab (on-demand)
- Full sweep grid (more concurrency points, more models/SKUs).
- Used for calibration and tier parameter tuning.

### Release candidate gating
- Requires at minimum:
  - Perf: W1–W7 across launch models/regions
  - Quality: Q1–Q4 on launch model(s)

---

## Versioning and change control
### Version semantics
- **v1** is the first standardized corpus for tiered batching defaults.
- Patch updates (v1.1, v1.2) are allowed for:
  - fixing broken prompts,
  - adjusting synthetic traces to match stable observed histograms,
  - adding targeted edge cases discovered during beta.

### Change approval
- Required reviewers for any corpus change:
  - Applied ML & Evals (Jonas Weber or Dr. Maya Srinivasan)
  - Serving Runtime scheduling lead (Sofia Ivanova) for perf-affecting changes
  - SRE/Observability (Allison Grant or Sean Gallagher) if metrics or thresholds interpretation changes

### Reproducibility requirements
Any corpus update must include:
- a changelog entry (what changed + why),
- a baseline run link (before/after) for at least one reference model/SKU,
- confirmation that prompt-length histograms remain within guardrails.

---

## Known limitations (v1)
- Tool-calling quality metrics are robust, but some prompts still exhibit model-version sensitivity; avoid using Q3 judge-based signals as sole gate.
- We do not yet include multilingual workloads as a first-class dimension.
- We do not include very large batch embeddings-only “offline indexing” workloads beyond W7; those will be added in v2 if customer demand increases.

---

## Appendix A — Canonical decoding settings (quality mode)
Unless a specific test case overrides, quality mode uses:
- temperature: 0.0
- top_p: 1.0
- max_tokens: per workload spec
- seed: fixed where supported
- repetition penalty: default

For Q3 (general chat), a smaller subset is run at temperature=0.2 to detect extreme sensitivity, but this is informational unless guardrails explicitly reference it.
